title: Prenatal exposure to maternal bereavement and childbirths in the offspring: a population-based cohort study.
ehr_evidence: The unique personal identification number, which is assigned to all live-born children and new residents, was used to link children to their relatives and to obtain information on demographic variables, vital statistics, health outcomes and socio-economic variables from different national registers.
summary: Population-based cohort study examining the association between prenatal exposure to maternal bereavement and fertility outcomes in offspring.
key_findings: No overall association between prenatal maternal bereavement and having a child (HR=0.98 [0.96–1.01] for males, HR=1.01 [0.98–1.03] for females).
Females born to mothers who lost a parent had a slightly reduced probability of having children (HR=0.97 [0.94–0.99]).
Females born to mothers who lost another child (HR=1.09 [1.04–1.14]), spouse (HR=1.29 [1.12–1.48]), or sibling (HR=1.13 [1.01–1.27]) had an increased probability.
Sudden death of a relative was associated with increased probability in females (HR=1.21 [1.14–1.29]).
No difference in age-specific mean number of childbirths between exposed and unexposed (HR=0.99 [0.96–1.01] males, HR=1.00 [0.98–1.02] females).
population: 2,112,770 males and 2,008,826 females born in Denmark (1968-1996) and Sweden (1973-1994), followed from age 12 to 41
limitations: inability to adjust for lifestyle factors or directly measure fecundity using registry data
follow-up only until age 41 does not cover full fertility life
incomplete linkage of mothers to relatives in early years in Denmark leading to exposure misclassification
potential for multiple testing false positives
possible confounding by postnatal paternal behavior
data_availability_statement: The authors confirm that, for approved reasons, some access restrictions apply to the data underlying the findings. All data is stored at the secure platform of Denmark Statistics, which is the central authority on Danish statistics with the mission to collect, compile and publish statisti cs on the Danish society. By legislations, researchers who want to get access to the data must apply for permissions from Both Statistics Denmark and Danish Data Prote ction Agency. Anyone with interests in this data can contact the authors of the study.
